title: Inventory Turnover: how fast stock moves
subtitle: Whether goods sell fast or slow - a signal of operating efficiency
openingQuestion: Inventory Turnover falls sharply while revenue rises slightly. What does that suggest?
openingOptions: Good - plenty of stock on hand and ready to sell to the customers next quarter
A warning - stock is building up faster than it sells, and may be going stale
explanation: Inventory turnover tells you how many times in a year a business sells through and restocks its inventory. Divide 365 by it and you get days of inventory, a figure that is easier to compare. The trend matters more than the absolute level: a turnover that keeps slowing means goods sit longer, more capital is locked up, and the risk of having to clear stock at a discount rises - in fashion or electronics, that is a loss waiting to be recognised.

diagram.label: Falling → goods selling slowly, inventory risk

realWorldExample.description: Zara is known for extremely fast inventory turnover thanks to its "fast fashion" model - designing, manufacturing and getting goods into stores within a few weeks, which minimises the risk of stock going out of fashion compared with traditional labels on far longer production cycles.

quiz.question: What does Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO) = 90 days mean?
options: Inventory turned over 90 times during the financial year
It takes 90 days on average to sell through a batch of stock
The business needs 90 days to finish manufacturing a batch
The business holds enough stock to sell for another 90 days
quiz.explanation: DIO = 365 / inventory turnover. A high DIO means goods sell slowly and capital is tied up longer. Compare against the industry: 90 days is fine for furniture, poor for food.

quiz.question: Why does inventory turnover matter more in fashion than in tinned food with a long shelf life?
options: Because fashion retailers rarely operate their own warehouses at all
Because tinned food carries a considerably higher profit margin
Because fashion loses value to trends even while still intact
Because a long shelf life keeps capital tied up markedly longer
quiz.explanation: Inventory risk comes not only from a physical expiry date but from an "economic expiry date" - in fashion, a shirt that has gone out of style can lose 50-70% of its value while remaining brand new.

quiz.question: COGS for the year is 1,800 billion and average inventory is 300 billion. What are inventory turnover and DIO?
options: 5 turns, DIO ≈ 73 days (= 1,500 ÷ 300, wrong COGS)
6 turns, DIO ≈ 30 days (= 180 ÷ 6, using half a year)
0.17 turns, DIO ≈ 2,190 days (numerator and denominator swapped)
6 turns, DIO ≈ 61 days (= 365 ÷ 6 turns)
quiz.explanation: Inventory turnover = COGS / average inventory = 1,800/300 = 6 turns. DIO = 365/6 ≈ 61 days. Each batch of stock sits in the warehouse for about two months before it sells.

quiz.question: A retailer's inventory turnover falls from 8 turns to 5 over two years. What is the main concern?
options: Stock is piling up and may need heavy discounting to clear
The business is running short of stock to meet demand
Storage costs fall because goods are moving more slowly
Gross margin will automatically rise along with turnover
quiz.explanation: Slowing turnover means goods sit in the warehouse longer: capital is buried, storage costs rise, and the likelihood of having to cut prices to free up space rises too - which comes straight out of next period's margin.

quiz.question: How does Zara's fast-fashion model affect this ratio?
options: Low turnover, because so many styles are held at once
Very high turnover, since stock enters and leaves in weeks
No change, because fast fashion only shortens the design stage
High turnover, but with a larger share of stock going stale
quiz.explanation: Cutting the product life cycle from months to weeks pushes inventory turnover very high, reducing both the capital tied up in the warehouse and the risk of going out of fashion - an operating advantage competitors find hard to copy.

keyTakeaways: A sharp fall = stock piling up - a warning signal
DIO = 365 / turnover - the average days to sell through stock

practicePrompt.question: A company has COGS = 900 billion a year and average inventory = 150 billion. What is its inventory turnover, and what does that figure tell you?
options: Inventory Turnover = COGS / average inventory = 900/150 = 6 times a year
Inventory Turnover = 150/900 = 0.17, the ratio of inventory to total production cost
Inventory Turnover = 900 − 150 = 750 billion, the goods sold during the year net of stock
Inventory Turnover means nothing unless the company is in retail
practicePrompt.explanation: Inventory turnover = COGS / average inventory = 900/150 = 6 times. The higher the figure, the faster goods move (less capital 'stuck' in the warehouse); a low figure can be a sign of slow-moving or stale stock, and should be watched alongside the revenue trend.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a sentence rather than as a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: A sharp fall = stock piling up - a warning signal

application.title: Work out an inventory turnover
application.message: Take COGS divided by average inventory for a retailer or manufacturer, then work out DIO (365/turnover) to see how many days it takes on average to sell through stock.
application.secondary: A DIO that jumps sharply from year to year is worth digging into.

sections.text: Inventory turnover measures how fast a business sells through its stock and replaces it - the faster goods sell, the less capital sits in the warehouse and the lower the risk of obsolescence.

sections.label: The formula
sections.text: Inventory Turnover = COGS / Average Inventory   |   Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO) = 365 / Inventory Turnover
What DIO tells you about a business

DIO = 90 days means the company takes 90 days on average to sell through a batch of stock. The figure only means something set against the industry standard: 90 days is normal, even good, for furniture (where purchase cycles are slow), but dreadful for fresh food (which needs to turn over within days).
Why Zara built an entire business model around fast turnover

Zara (Inditex) is known for its "fast fashion" model: designing, manufacturing and getting goods into stores within a few weeks rather than the several months traditional labels take. The reason is that fashion loses value quickly as trends move - even with no physical expiry, a shirt that has gone out of style can lose 50-70% of its value. For tinned food with a long shelf life that risk is far lower, so inventory turnover matters correspondingly less.

items: Inventory turnover falling steadily = goods selling more slowly, or stock accumulating - a warning signal
The attendant risks: having to discount heavily to move stock, or having to write down inventory value, which hits profit directly
Inventory turnover must be compared within an industry - fashion retail is nothing like furniture or tinned food
An "economic expiry date" (value lost to fashion or obsolescence) is sometimes more dangerous than a physical one

lines: Fast inventory turnover doesn't just save working capital - for some industries, it is what makes the whole business model viable.
